metadata.chapter_title: Bivariate Data, Time Series, and Linear Regression (10 & 10A)
metadata.title: Scatterplots, Lines of Best Fit, and Time-Series Data
metadata.vcaa_description: Construct scatterplots and comment on the association between the 2 numerical variables; fit a line of best fit and make predictions (including time series VC2M10ST04, VC2M10ST05, and 10A least-squares VC2M10AST02).
metadata.target_mastery: Describe bivariate associations (direction, form, strength), fit and interpret a linear model $y = mx + c$, distinguish between reliable interpolation and risky extrapolation, analyse time-series trends and moving averages, and apply Pearson's correlation coefficient $r$ and the least-squares regression line $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$ (10A).
prerequisites: Equations and gradients of straight lines $y = mx + c$ (Year 9/10)

key_vocabulary.definition: In bivariate analysis, the explanatory (independent) variable $x$ is plotted on the horizontal axis and is used to explain or predict changes in the response (dependent) variable $y$ plotted on the vertical axis.

Interpolation is using a line of best fit to predict $y$ for an $x$-value within the range of the observed data (generally reliable); extrapolation is predicting beyond the minimum or maximum observed $x$-values (unreliable because the linear trend may not continue).

key_vocabulary.term: Time-series plot, secular trend, and seasonality
key_vocabulary.definition: A bivariate line graph where the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis is time $t$; a long-term upward or downward direction is a secular trend, while regular repeating fluctuations across a fixed period (such as summer/winter quarters) represent seasonality.

key_vocabulary.term: Pearson's correlation coefficient ($r$) and least-squares regression (10A)
key_vocabulary.definition: A dimensionless measure $-1 \le r \le 1$ of the strength and direction of a linear association; the least-squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$ minimises the sum of squared vertical residuals $\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$, with slope $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$ and intercept $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$.

theory.title: Scatterplots, Lines of Best Fit, and Interpreting Gradient and Intercept in Context
theory.explanation: A scatterplot displays paired observations $(x_i, y_i)$ of two numerical variables. We describe a bivariate association by its direction (positive or negative), form (linear or non-linear), and strength (strong, moderate, weak, or none). When a linear association exists, we fit a straight line of best fit $y = mx + c$. In real-world modelling, the gradient $m$ represents the average change in the response variable $y$ for each $1$-unit increase in the explanatory variable $x$, and the $y$-intercept $c$ represents the predicted value of $y$ when $x = 0$. Predictions inside the observed domain $[x_{\min}, x_{\max}]$ are called interpolation (reliable), whereas predictions outside $[x_{\min}, x_{\max}]$ are called extrapolation (risky and potentially meaningless).
theory.callout_rule: Even a strong linear association between $x$ and $y$ (such as ice-cream sales and surf lifesaving rescues) does not prove that $x$ causes $y$ — both may be driven by a third confounding (lurking) variable such as hot summer temperature.

theory.title: Time-Series Data: Secular Trends, Seasonality, and Moving Averages
theory.explanation: A time-series plot records a numerical variable over equally spaced time intervals (hours, months, quarters, or years) with consecutive points joined by line segments. Time-series patterns include: (1) a secular trend (long-term upward or downward movement), (2) seasonal variation (predictable calendar-linked peaks and troughs within each year), and (3) random irregular noise. To smooth out short-term fluctuations and reveal the underlying trend, we calculate a $k$-point moving average (such as a $3$-point or $5$-point moving average) by averaging each consecutive window of $k$ observations.
theory.formula_latex: \text{3-point moving average at time } t = \frac{y_{t-1} + y_t + y_{t+1}}{3}
theory.callout_title: Moving Averages Smooth Out Seasonal Spikes
theory.callout_rule: To smooth quarterly data across a $4$-quarter year (or $3$-month seasons), averaging consecutive groups damps out the seasonal peaks and troughs so the underlying long-term trend becomes clear.

theory.title: [10A] Pearson's Correlation Coefficient ($r$) and Least-Squares Regression
theory.explanation: In Year 10A (VC2M10AST02), the strength and direction of a linear relationship are quantified by Pearson's correlation coefficient $r \in [-1, 1]$: $r = +1$ is a perfect positive linear fit, $r = 0$ indicates no linear correlation, and $r = -1$ is a perfect negative linear fit (values with $|r| \ge 0.75$ are typically classified as strong, $0.50 \le |r| < 0.75$ as moderate, and $0.25 \le |r| < 0.50$ as weak). The unique least-squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$ minimises the sum of squared vertical residuals $\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$, always passes through the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, and has gradient $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$ and $y$-intercept $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$.
theory.formula_latex: b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}, \qquad \hat{y} = a + bx
theory.callout_title: The Least-Squares Line Always Passes Through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$
theory.callout_rule: Once you calculate the least-squares slope $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$, substitute the sample means $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ into $\bar{y} = a + b\bar{x}$ to find the vertical intercept $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$.

worked_examples.title: Fitting a Line of Best Fit, Interpreting Parameters, and Interpolation vs Extrapolation
worked_examples.problem: An environmental scientist measures the dissolved oxygen concentration $y$ (in $\text{mg/L}$) in a Murray River billabong at water temperatures $x$ (in $^\circ\text{C}$) ranging from $x = 10^\circ\text{C}$ to $x = 30^\circ\text{C}$. A line of best fit passes through $(10, 11.0)$ and $(25, 8.0)$. Find: (a) the equation of the line of best fit $y = mx + c$ and interpret $m$ in context, (b) the predicted dissolved oxygen at $x = 20^\circ\text{C}$, and (c) the residual for an actual measurement of $(20, 9.4)$ and whether predicting at $x = 20^\circ\text{C}$ or $x = 45^\circ\text{C}$ is more reliable.

steps.thinking: Calculate the gradient $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ from $(10, 11.0)$ and $(25, 8.0)$, then substitute $(10, 11.0)$ to find $c$.
steps.working:
$$m = \frac{8.0 - 11.0}{25 - 10} = \frac{-3.0}{15} = -0.2\text{ mg/L per } ^\circ\text{C}$$
$$11.0 = -0.2(10) + c \implies c = 13.0 \implies \hat{y} = -0.2x + 13.0$$
$$\text{Interpretation: Dissolved oxygen decreases by an average of } 0.2\text{ mg/L for each } 1^\circ\text{C rise in water temperature.}$$

steps.thinking: Evaluate $\text{Residual} = y_{\text{actual}} - \hat{y}_{\text{predicted}} = 9.4 - 9.0$, and compare $x = 20^\circ\text{C}$ vs $x = 45^\circ\text{C}$ against the data domain $[10^\circ\text{C}, 30^\circ\text{C}]$.
steps.working:
$$\text{Residual} = 9.4 - 9.0 = +0.4\text{ mg/L}$$
$$x = 20^\circ\text{C} \text{ lies inside } [10, 30] \text{ (reliable interpolation), whereas } x = 45^\circ\text{C} \text{ is outside } [10, 30] \text{ (unreliable extrapolation).}$$

worked_examples.final_answer: (a) $\hat{y} = -0.2x + 13.0$ ($y$ decreases by $0.2\text{ mg/L}$ per $1^\circ\text{C}$); (b) $9.0\text{ mg/L}$; (c) residual $= +0.4\text{ mg/L}$, and $x = 20^\circ\text{C}$ (interpolation) is reliable whereas $x = 45^\circ\text{C}$ (extrapolation) is not

now_you_try.problem: A line of best fit relating study time $x$ (in hours, observed for $1 \le x \le 8$) and quiz score $\hat{y}$ (out of $50$) passes through $(2, 24)$ and $(6, 40)$. Find (a) the equation $\hat{y} = mx + c$, and (b) the predicted score at $x = 5$ hours.

worked_examples.title: Time-Series Analysis and 3-Point Moving Averages
worked_examples.problem: A solar energy retailer in Mildura records the number of rooftop solar installations over $5$ consecutive months (Months $1$ to $5$): $18, 24, 21, 27, 30$. Find: (a) the $3$-point moving averages centred at Month $2$, Month $3$, and Month $4$, and (b) describe the underlying secular trend revealed by the smoothed values.

steps.thinking: Average each consecutive window of $3$ months: Months $(1,2,3)$ for Month $2$, Months $(2,3,4)$ for Month $3$, and Months $(3,4,5)$ for Month $4$.
Examine the progression of the smoothed moving averages $21 \to 24 \to 26$.
steps.working: $$\text{Although raw installations dipped in Month 3 (from } 24 \text{ to } 21\text{), the smoothed 3-point moving averages } (21, 24, 26) \text{ show a steady upward (increasing) secular trend.}$$

now_you_try.problem: Daily visitors to a gallery from Monday to Friday are $110, 140, 125, 155, 170$. Calculate the $3$-point moving averages for Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday.
now_you_try.hint: Average $(\text{Mon, Tue, Wed})$, $(\text{Tue, Wed, Thu})$, and $(\text{Wed, Thu, Fri})$.

worked_examples.title: [10A] Least-Squares Regression Line from Summary Statistics
worked_examples.problem: A study of $n = 20$ second-hand cars of the same model records their age $x$ (in years) and resale price $y$ (in $\$\text{thousands}$). The summary statistics are: $\bar{x} = 5$, $s_x = 2$, $\bar{y} = 22$, $s_y = 6$, and Pearson's correlation coefficient is $r = -0.85$. Find: (a) the gradient $b$ and vertical intercept $a$ of the least-squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$, and (b) the predicted resale price of a $4$-year-old car.

steps.thinking: Substitute $r = -0.85$, $s_y = 6$, and $s_x = 2$ into the least-squares slope formula $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$.
Use the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = (5, 22)$ in $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$ to find the vertical intercept $a$.

now_you_try.problem: For bivariate data with $\bar{x} = 10$, $s_x = 4$, $\bar{y} = 50$, $s_y = 10$, and $r = 0.80$, find the equation of the least-squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$.

common_misconceptions.title: Assuming Correlation Implies Direct Causation
common_misconceptions.misconception: Concluding that because two variables have a correlation coefficient close to $1$ (e.g. $r = 0.92$), changing $x$ directly causes $y$ to change.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Correlation measures statistical association only. A strong correlation between $x$ and $y$ is often produced by a common confounding (lurking) variable $z$ that drives both $x$ and $y$, or by coincidence.
common_misconceptions.correct_working: $$\text{High summer UV radiation (confounding variable) independently increases both sunglasses sales and sunburn cases.}$$
common_misconceptions.counter_example: Banning sunglasses would not reduce sunburns.

common_misconceptions.title: Swapping $s_x$ and $s_y$ in the Least-Squares Slope Formula $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Just like the gradient of any line is $\frac{\text{rise } (\Delta y)}{\text{run } (\Delta x)}$, the vertical spread $s_y$ is always on top (numerator) and the horizontal spread $s_x$ is always on the bottom (denominator): $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$.
common_misconceptions.correct_working: $$b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x} \quad \left(\text{units of } b = \frac{\text{units of } y}{\text{units of } x}\right)$$
common_misconceptions.counter_example: Checking units immediately catches this error: if $y$ is in dollars and $x$ is in hours, the slope $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$ has units of dollars per hour.

fluency_and_understanding.question: A line of best fit passes through the points $(4, 15)$ and $(12, 39)$. Find (a) its gradient $m$, (b) its $y$-intercept $c$, and (c) the predicted value $\hat{y}$ when $x = 10$.
step_by_step_solution: Substitute $(4, 15)$ into $y = 3x + c$: $15 = 12 + c \implies c = 3$, so $\hat{y} = 3x + 3$ and $\hat{y}(10) = 3(10) + 3 = 33$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: A linear regression model for plant height $\hat{y}$ (in $\text{cm}$) after $x$ weeks of growth is $\hat{y} = 2.5x + 6$. If a plant at $x = 8$ weeks has an actual measured height of $y = 24.5\text{ cm}$, find (a) the predicted height $\hat{y}(8)$, and (b) the residual $e = y - \hat{y}$.
step_by_step_solution: Substitute $x = 8$ into $\hat{y} = 2.5(8) + 6 = 20 + 6 = 26\text{ cm}$.
Calculate the residual: $e = y_{\text{actual}} - \hat{y}_{\text{predicted}} = 24.5 - 26 = -1.5\text{ cm}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Quarterly electricity bills (in $\$$) for a household over $5$ quarters ($Q_1$ to $Q_5$) are: $320, 410, 500, 350, 340$. Calculate the $3$-point moving averages centred at $Q_2$, $Q_3$, and $Q_4$.

[10A] Classify the direction and strength of the linear association represented by each value of Pearson's correlation coefficient: (a) $r = 0.91$, (b) $r = -0.62$, (c) $r = 0.04$, and (d) $r = -0.99$.
fluency_and_understanding.final_answer: (a) Strong positive, (b) Moderate negative, (c) Virtually no linear correlation, (d) Very strong (almost perfect) negative
step_by_step_solution: The sign of $r$ gives the direction ($+$ positive, $-$ negative) and $|r|$ gives the strength.

Thus $0.91$ is strong positive ($|r| \ge 0.75$), $-0.62$ is moderate negative ($0.50 \le |r| < 0.75$), $0.04$ indicates virtually no linear relationship ($|r| \approx 0$), and $-0.99$ is a very strong negative linear relationship.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A barista tracks daily hot chocolate sales $y$ (cups) against the daily maximum temperature $x$ (in $^\circ\text{C}$, recorded for temperatures between $8^\circ\text{C}$ and $28^\circ\text{C}$) and obtains the linear model $\hat{y} = 140 - 4x$. (a) Interpret the gradient $-4$ and $y$-intercept $140$ in context. (b) Predict sales on a $15^\circ\text{C}$ day and on a $40^\circ\text{C}$ heatwave day, and explain why the $40^\circ\text{C}$ prediction makes no physical sense.
problem_solving_and_modelling.final_answer: (a) Sales drop by $4$ cups per $1^\circ\text{C}$ increase, with $140$ cups predicted at $0^\circ\text{C}$; (b) $\hat{y}(15) = 80$ cups (reliable interpolation), whereas $\hat{y}(40) = -20$ cups (impossible negative sales caused by extrapolating far beyond $28^\circ\text{C}$)
step_by_step_solution: At $x = 15^\circ\text{C}$ (interpolation inside $[8, 28]$), $\hat{y}(15) = 140 - 4(15) = 80$ cups.
At $x = 40^\circ\text{C}$ (extrapolation above $28^\circ\text{C}$), $\hat{y}(40) = 140 - 4(40) = -20$ cups, which is impossible because cup sales cannot be negative.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: An alpine ski resort at Mount Buller records quarterly visitor numbers (in thousands) across a year: Q1 (Summer) $= 15$, Q2 (Autumn) $= 25$, Q3 (Winter) $= 140$, Q4 (Spring) $= 20$, and in the following year Q1 $= 19$. Find (a) the $4$-quarter mean visitor number for the first year, and (b) the $4$-quarter moving average when Q1 of the first year ($15$) is replaced by Q1 of the second year ($19$), and state what this indicates about the year-on-year trend.
problem_solving_and_modelling.final_answer: (a) $50$ thousand per quarter, (b) $51$ thousand per quarter (an upward year-on-year trend)
step_by_step_solution: For the first four quarters, the mean is $\frac{15 + 25 + 140 + 20}{4} = \frac{200}{4} = 50$ thousand.
For the shifted $4$-quarter window $(25, 140, 20, 19)$, the mean is $\frac{25 + 140 + 20 + 19}{4} = \frac{204}{4} = 51$ thousand, showing an upward trend once seasonal winter spikes are smoothed.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: [10A] In a sports science study of $n = 30$ rowers, arm span $x$ (in $\text{cm}$) and peak rowing power $y$ (in Watts) have summary statistics $\bar{x} = 180$, $s_x = 8$, $\bar{y} = 420$, $s_y = 40$, and $r = 0.75$. Find (a) the slope $b$ and intercept $a$ of the least-squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$, and (b) the predicted peak power for a rower with an arm span of $192\text{ cm}$.
step_by_step_solution: Calculate $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x} = 0.75 \times \frac{40}{8} = 0.75 \times 5 = 3.75\text{ W/cm}$ and $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} = 420 - 3.75(180) = 420 - 675 = -255\text{ W}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: [10A] Calculate the exact least-squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$ and Pearson's correlation coefficient $r$ for the $n = 3$ data points $(1, 2), (3, 5), (5, 8)$.
problem_solving_and_modelling.final_answer: $\hat{y} = 0.5 + 1.5x$ and $r = 1$ (since all $3$ points lie on a straight line of positive gradient $1.5$)
step_by_step_solution: Because the gradient between $(1, 2)$, $(3, 5)$, and $(5, 8)$ is constant ($b = \frac{5 - 2}{3 - 1} = 1.5$), the points are perfectly collinear with $r = 1$, $b = 1 \times \frac{3}{2} = 1.5$, and $a = 5 - 1.5(3) = 0.5$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: [10A] Prove using the formula $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$ that for ANY dataset, the point of means $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ always lies exactly on the least-squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Substituting $x = \bar{x}$ into $\hat{y} = a + bx = (\bar{y} - b\bar{x}) + b\bar{x}$ simplifies immediately to $\hat{y}(\bar{x}) = \bar{y}$
step_by_step_solution: Write the equation of the least-squares line as $\hat{y} = a + bx$ where $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$.
Evaluate $\hat{y}$ at $x = \bar{x}$: $\hat{y}(\bar{x}) = (\bar{y} - b\bar{x}) + b\bar{x} = \bar{y}$, proving that $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ always lies on the regression line.

reasoning_and_communication.question: In a coastal town, a data analyst discovers a strong positive correlation ($r = 0.88$) between monthly sunscreen sales and monthly shark sightings. Explain why it would be a statistical error to claim that buying sunscreen attracts sharks, and identify the confounding variable.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Summer weather / warmer water temperatures (the confounding variable) independently causes more people to buy sunscreen and go swimming at the beach AND more sharks/spotters to be active near shore
step_by_step_solution: Correlation does not imply causation: sunscreen sales do not physically influence shark behaviour.
The lurking/confounding variable is seasonal summer temperature, which drives both higher beach attendance (increasing sunscreen sales and human observation) and coastal marine activity.

reasoning_and_communication.question: [10A] Use the formula $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$ to explain why the sign of the least-squares gradient $b$ is always identical to the sign of Pearson's correlation coefficient $r$, and why $r = 0$ always yields a horizontal regression line $\hat{y} = \bar{y}$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Since standard deviations $s_x > 0$ and $s_y > 0$ are always positive, $\frac{s_y}{s_x} > 0$, so $b$ and $r$ have the exact same sign; when $r = 0$, $b = 0$ and $a = \bar{y} - 0 = \bar{y}$, giving the horizontal line $\hat{y} = \bar{y}$
step_by_step_solution: Because sample standard deviations $s_x$ and $s_y$ are positive square roots ($s_x > 0, s_y > 0$), their ratio $\frac{s_y}{s_x}$ is strictly positive, so $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$ has the same sign as $r$.
If $r = 0$, then $b = 0 \times \frac{s_y}{s_x} = 0$ and $a = \bar{y} - 0(\bar{x}) = \bar{y}$, so the best linear predictor is simply the constant horizontal mean line $\hat{y} = \bar{y}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: [10A] A student fits two models to the $3$ data points $(1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 5)$: Model 1 is the horizontal line $\hat{y} = 4$ (the mean $\bar{y}$), and Model 2 is the least-squares line $\hat{y} = 1 + 1.5x$. Calculate the Sum of Squared Residuals $\text{SSR} = \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$ for both models and verify that the least-squares line achieves a much smaller $\text{SSR}$.
